title: Why the French Revolution started
summary: You know the Bastille and the three estates. See how a royal debt crisis and a fight over voting rules became a revolution in 1789.
objective: Explain how the crown's debt and the voting fight in the Estates-General turned a money problem into a revolution, and correct the 'hungry mob' version.

hook.prompt: The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789. Who set the revolution's chain of events in motion a year before that?

options.text: Hungry Parisians rioting over bread prices
options.feedback: Bread mattered, but it came later in the chain. The first move was made at the top.

options.text: Radical writers calling for a republic
options.feedback: Almost no one was calling for a republic in 1788. The first move came from someone with far more power.

hook.explanation: In 1788 the nearly bankrupt crown itself called the Estates-General. How a money problem became a revolution is what this lesson unpacks.

bricks.title: It started with money
bricks.body: Revolutions are often pictured as hunger boiling over. France's began with money. Wars, including aid to the American Revolution, left the crown so indebted that interest took about half its spending. Nobles and clergy paid little direct tax. When ministers tried to tax them in 1787, they refused and demanded the **Estates-General**, unused since 1614. In August 1788 a nearly bankrupt king agreed to summon it.

term.definition: France's old assembly of the three orders: clergy (First Estate), nobles (Second Estate), and everyone else (Third Estate).

visual.alt: A chain of three steps: war debt, then tax reform blocked by nobles and clergy, then the Estates-General summoned in 1788.
visual.html:
War debt: interest eats about half the budget
↓
1787: nobles and clergy refuse new taxes
↓
1788: the king summons the Estates-General

bricks.prompt: Suppose the crown had carried little debt in 1788, but everything else stayed the same. By this lesson's chain, what would most likely be missing?

options.text: A reason to summon the Estates-General
The nobles' and clergy's light tax burden
options.feedback: Their privileges existed either way. They only became a crisis once a debt-ridden crown needed their money.

options.text: Nothing: the same chain would follow
options.feedback: In this chain, debt is the first link. Without it, there's no tax fight with the privileged and no need to call an assembly.

bricks.explanation: No debt, no urgent need to tax the privileged, no blocked reform, and so no reason for the king to call an assembly he'd avoided since 1614.

bricks.title: The voting fight made it a revolution
bricks.body: When the Estates-General met in May 1789, the Third Estate had as many deputies as the other two combined. But if each estate voted **by order**, as one block, clergy and nobles could still win 2 to 1. The Third demanded voting **by head**. On 17 June 1789 its deputies declared themselves the **National Assembly**: they, not the king, spoke for the nation. In July, with bread scarce and troops massing near Paris, crowds armed themselves and stormed the Bastille.

term.definition: Every deputy gets one vote, instead of each estate casting a single block vote.

visual.alt: Deputies in round numbers: clergy 300, nobles 300, Third Estate 600. By order the vote is 2 estates to 1; by head it is 600 to 600.
visual.html:
Clergy
300
Nobles
300
Third Estate
600
By order: 2 votes to 1By head: 600 to 600

bricks.prompt: Round numbers: clergy 300, nobles 300, Third Estate 600 deputies. A reform wins all 600 Third Estate votes, 140 clergy and 90 nobles. How does it fare?

options.text: Loses by order; passes by head

options.feedback: By head it passes, but by order the clergy (140 of 300) and nobles (90 of 300) each cast one block vote against it.
By order it loses, but by head 600 + 140 + 90 = 830 of 1,200 is a clear majority.

options.text: Passes by order; loses by head
options.feedback: That's reversed: the block vote is what lets the two smaller estates outvote the Third.

bricks.hint: Under voting by order, find each estate's majority first.
bricks.explanation:
By order: clergy (140 of 300) and nobles (90 of 300) vote no, 2 to 1.
By head: 830 of 1,200 vote yes.

bricks.prompt: Why was the deputies' declaration on 17 June 1789 revolutionary in itself, weeks before any fighting?

options.text: It claimed the right to decide for the nation without the king's consent
It removed the king from the throne
options.feedback: The king kept his throne. The claim was about who speaks for the nation, not about removing him.

options.text: It gave the Third Estate more seats
options.feedback: It already had as many seats as the other two combined. Seats didn't help while each estate voted as one block.

options.text: It ended the nobles' tax privileges
options.feedback: Taxes were the starting problem, but this declaration was about something bigger: who has the right to decide at all.

bricks.explanation: Calling themselves the National Assembly, the deputies claimed to speak for the whole nation, so they no longer needed the king's or the other orders' consent.

challenge.situation: At a quiz night, a friend sums it up: "The French Revolution started when starving Parisians stormed the Bastille." You get one sentence to set it straight.

options.text: "Hunger mattered, but a broke crown had already called the Estates-General, and its deputies declared the National Assembly weeks before the Bastille fell."
options.outcome: Your friend gets the whole chain: debt opened the door, the voting fight made it a revolution, and the July crowds came after.

options.text: "It wasn't about hunger at all; it was the king's debts."
options.outcome: You've named the first link, but you've dropped the crowds, and debt alone doesn't explain deputies claiming to speak for the nation.

options.text: "Right, the Bastille is where it all began."
options.outcome: The myth survives. By 14 July the king had summoned the Estates-General and the Third Estate had declared itself the National Assembly.

challenge.hint: Which happened first: the National Assembly or the Bastille?
challenge.explanation: The Bastille was a late link. Debt forced the Estates-General, the voting fight produced the National Assembly, and only then did hungry, fearful crowds take up arms.

takeaways: Start with the money: the crown's debt is why an assembly met at all in 1789.
The fight over voting by order or by head turned a tax problem into a claim that the nation, not the king, decides.
The Bastille came after the National Assembly; the crowds acted in a revolution already declared.
